exams.title: Global Success 12 – Unit 8: Wildlife Conservation – Test 1: Ngữ pháp & Từ vựng (15 câu)

qs.q:
UNIT 8: WILDLIFE CONSERVATION — NGỮ PHÁP & TỪ VỰNG (ĐỀ 1): Mark the letter A, B, C, or D on your answer sheet to indicate the correct answer to each of the following questions.
______ strict anti-poaching laws are enforced immediately, critically endangered gibbons could become extinct in the wild.
qs.ex: Ngữ pháp Unit 8 Lớp 12 (Adverbial clauses of condition): 'Unless' (= If... not: Trừ khi luật chống săn trộm nghiêm ngặt được thực thi...).

qs.q: Rescued primates are released back into the forest only ______ they can find food and avoid predators on their own.
qs.ex: 'provided that / as long as' = với điều kiện là, miễn là.

qs.q: Today, the population of wild tigers in Southeast Asia is not so large ______ it was fifty years ago.
qs.ex: Ngữ pháp Unit 8 (Adverbial clauses of comparison): So sánh không bằng 'not so/as + adj + as'.

qs.q: Illegal hunting, also known as ______, is the greatest threat to rhinos, elephants and pangolins.
qs.ex: Từ vựng Unit 8: poaching = nạn săn bắn trộm động vật hoang dã.

qs.q: Coral reefs are ______ more sensitive to rising ocean temperatures than many people realise.
qs.ex: Nhấn mạnh cấp so sánh hơn: 'much / far + more + adj + than'.

qs.q: You can visit the sea-turtle nesting beach at night ______ you do not use flash photography or loud lights.
qs.ex: Mệnh đề điều kiện: 'as long as / so long as' = miễn là.

qs.q: The Cat Ba langur is listed as ______ endangered because fewer than a hundred individuals remain in the wild.
qs.ex: Từ vựng Unit 8: critically endangered = cực kỳ nguy cấp (bậc cao nhất trước khi tuyệt chủng).

qs.q: Injured gibbons are cared for in spacious forest ______ at the rescue centre before being returned to nature.
qs.ex: Từ vựng Unit 8: enclosures = khu nuôi nhốt bán hoang dã có rào bảo vệ.

qs.q: Penalties for smuggling ivory and rhino horn should be ______ stricter than they are today.
qs.ex: Nhấn mạnh so sánh hơn: far stricter than...

qs.q: Many rare primates bred in ______ struggle to survive in the wild unless they are trained to forage for fruit and leaves.
qs.ex: Từ vựng Unit 8: in captivity = trong điều kiện nuôi nhốt.

qs.q: ______ local villagers are given sustainable jobs in ecotourism, some may still rely on forest hunting for income.
qs.ex: 'Unless' (= Nếu người dân địa phương không được tạo sinh kế bền vững...).

qs.q: Rangers use camera traps and GPS collars to ______ the movement of released bears across the national park.
qs.ex: Từ vựng Unit 8: monitor = theo dõi, giám sát.

qs.q: Restoring a degraded mangrove forest takes ______ longer than cutting it down for shrimp ponds.
qs.ex: Nhấn mạnh so sánh hơn: much longer than...

qs.q: Once the baby sea turtles hatch on the sand, volunteers protect them ______ they reach the ocean safely.
qs.ex: Liên từ thời gian/điều kiện hoàn tất: until.

qs.q: Clearing tropical forests for timber causes severe habitat ______, leaving arboreal apes with nowhere to live.
qs.ex: Từ vựng Unit 8: habitat loss = sự mất sinh cảnh sống.

**SAVE ENDANGERED WILDLIFE – ACT NOW!**
Right now, our school and community **(1)**______ a special campaign focused on protecting endangered wildlife, rehabilitating primates and sea turtles, and we invite everyone to join us. Many conservationists and rangers regularly participate in conservation programmes in nature reserves and rescue centres, where **(2)**______ a positive difference every week. Taking part in these activities helps young people learn how to rescue poached primates and sea turtles and release them back into the wild. Educators and families also note that **(3)**______ protect forest habitats and enforce strict anti-poaching laws. This month, our organisers **(4)**______ practical workshops on how to conserve endangered wildlife and their natural habitats, so please **(5)**______ the activities in your neighbourhood. Your active **(6)**______ will help build a better future for everyone!
(Adapted from Global Success – Unit 8: Wildlife Conservation)

qs.q:
Mark the letter A, B, C or D on your answer sheet to indicate the best arrangement of utterances or sentences to make a cohesive and coherent exchange or text in each of the following questions from 7 to 11.
**Dear Alex,**
a. At school, our teachers also organise practical projects to help us rescue poached primates and sea turtles and release them back into the wild.
b. Thank you for your email; it was great to hear about your recent school activities.
c. At weekends, my friends and I join community groups to conserve endangered wildlife and their natural habitats in nature reserves and rescue centres.
d. I’m writing to tell you about how we are learning about protecting endangered wildlife, rehabilitating primates and sea turtles in Unit 8: Wildlife Conservation.
e. Write back soon and tell me what your school is doing on this topic!
**Best wishes,**
qs.ex: Trình tự bức thư: Cảm ơn thư trước (b) → Nêu lý do viết thư chia sẻ chủ đề Unit (d) → Kể hoạt động ở trường (a) → Kể hoạt động cuối tuần (c) → Lời kết thư (e): b - d - a - c - e.

qs.q:
a. Nam: Yes, definitely! Let’s sign up together after class today.
b. Mai: Nam, our school club is holding a workshop on protecting endangered wildlife, rehabilitating primates and sea turtles this Saturday. Would you like to join?
c. Mai: Great! I’ll get two registration forms from the club leader.
qs.ex: Trình tự hội thoại 3 lượt: Mai rủ Nam tham gia workshop chủ đề Unit (b) → Nam đồng ý đăng ký (a) → Mai nói sẽ đi lấy phiếu đăng ký (c): b - a - c.

qs.q:
a. To address this, schools and communities are now launching new conservation programmes in nature reserves and rescue centres.
b. In the past, many people did not pay enough attention to protecting endangered wildlife, rehabilitating primates and sea turtles.
c. Today, however, both conservationists and rangers realise how important it is to conserve endangered wildlife and their natural habitats.
d. As a result, everyone benefits when we work together to protect forest habitats and enforce strict anti-poaching laws.
e. These practical programmes help participants rescue poached primates and sea turtles and release them back into the wild in their daily lives.

**PERSPECTIVES ON WILDLIFE CONSERVATION**
In recent years, protecting endangered wildlife, rehabilitating primates and sea turtles has attracted growing attention from educators and researchers alike. A recent national survey reports that while over eighty per cent of conservationists and rangers recognise the importance of conservation programmes, only about thirty-five per cent have <u>**rescued**</u> these practices into their daily routines in nature reserves and rescue centres. Even when resources are available, many people still struggle to balance their busy schedules with the need to conserve endangered wildlife and their natural habitats.
The challenge lies not only in awareness but also in daily habits. Researchers note that active participants regularly engage in structured tasks that rescue poached primates and sea turtles and release them back into the wild, whereas passive observers only join occasional events once or twice a year. Consistent practice requires patience and planning, but it delivers lasting rewards. Many individuals simply repeat outdated habits they observed in the past, which prevents them from experiencing how conservation programmes can protect forest habitats and enforce strict anti-poaching laws.
Fortunately, attitudes are shifting rapidly. **[I]** Most respondents in the survey agreed that everyone should conserve endangered wildlife and their natural habitats, even though many admitted spending less than two hours a week on it themselves. **[II]** Progress was strongest in communities where schools and families worked together as partners. **[III]** Groups can begin by setting clear weekly goals and giving every member a practical role in nature reserves and rescue centres. **[IV]** Small, steady steps like these can turn a difficult challenge into a shared habit of cooperation.
Promoting protecting endangered wildlife, rehabilitating primates and sea turtles matters for the long-term future. Young people who see conservationists and rangers model positive behaviours are likely to view these practices as normal, and <u>**they**</u> will carry those values into adulthood. In this way, conservation programmes not only rescue poached primates and sea turtles and release them back into the wild today but also protect forest habitats and enforce strict anti-poaching laws for generations to come.
(Adapted from Educational & Social Research Reports – Unit 8: Wildlife Conservation)

**MAKING WILDLIFE CONSERVATION PART OF DAILY LIFE**
Taking time to conserve endangered wildlife and their natural habitats may seem ordinary at first glance, yet a growing body of research highlights its transformative power. Studies show that well-designed conservation programmes help conservationists and rangers rescue poached primates and sea turtles and release them back into the wild. At the same time, these practices protect forest habitats and enforce strict anti-poaching laws and foster stronger cooperation in nature reserves and rescue centres.
Despite these clear advantages, participation in conservation programmes has faced obstacles in recent years. Researchers report that <u>**they**</u> have been neglected in many busy communities due to modern time pressures. <u>**Tight timetables, heavy workloads and a lack of practical guidance can all prevent people from maintaining positive routines.**</u> Even when individuals want to improve, distractions often get in the way.
The encouraging news is that success does not require perfection from day one. Experts emphasise that building <u>**vulnerable**</u> habits is about steady progress rather than instant results. Conservationists and rangers can start with simple steps in nature reserves and rescue centres, share responsibilities and use practical checklists to stay on track. Those who understand the purpose behind protecting endangered wildlife, rehabilitating primates and sea turtles become much more resilient and motivated.
Of course, no single workshop or rule will solve every challenge overnight, and some groups need time to adapt. That is no reason to give up. Even one or two focused sessions a week can spark meaningful change, and the positive <u>**enclosure**</u> will grow stronger over time. What matters most is the commitment people bring to supporting one another every day.
(Adapted from Global Success Reading Series – Unit 8: Wildlife Conservation)

**PARTNERSHIPS BETWEEN SCHOOLS AND FAMILIES IN UNIT 8: WILDLIFE CONSERVATION**
Over the past two years, a research team from the National Institute of Education has tracked 1,500 high school students to evaluate how protecting endangered wildlife, rehabilitating primates and sea turtles affects teenager development. The study found that while nearly ninety per cent of conservationists and rangers valued conservation programmes, only forty-two per cent <u>**sustained**</u> these routines throughout the entire school year. Students who tried to practise alone often gave up after a few weeks when exam pressure increased.
By contrast, learners whose families and teachers coordinated their guidance achieved far more durable results. In households where parents actively joined weekend activities to conserve endangered wildlife and their natural habitats in nature reserves and rescue centres, teenagers were twice as likely to rescue poached primates and sea turtles and release them back into the wild. Researchers explained that shared routines reduce the feeling of isolation and turn abstract classroom advice into enjoyable daily habits. Moreover, consistent family involvement helps protect forest habitats and enforce strict anti-poaching laws without adding extra stress to students’ timetables.
Schools across the country are now redesigning their programmes based on these findings. **[I]** Instead of assigning theoretical worksheets, teachers invite parents and students to co-sign a simple weekly action plan. **[II]** This joint commitment ensures that classroom lessons are reinforced at home every evening. **[III]** At monthly review sessions, classes celebrate collective progress and exchange practical solutions to common obstacles. **[IV]**
The long-term implications of this partnership model are encouraging. When conservationists and rangers work side by side, <u>**they**</u> build mutual respect and lasting life skills. Ultimately, integrating protecting endangered wildlife, rehabilitating primates and sea turtles into both school curricula and family life prepares young citizens to thrive in an increasingly complex world.
(Adapted from National Educational Research Reports – Unit 8: Wildlife Conservation)

**WHY CONSISTENCY MATTERS MORE THAN PERFECTION IN UNIT 8: WILDLIFE CONSERVATION**
When people first decide to focus on protecting endangered wildlife, rehabilitating primates and sea turtles, they often set overly ambitious targets. Enthusiastic beginners might promise to transform their entire lifestyle in a single weekend, only to feel exhausted a few days later. Studies on habit formation show that well-paced conservation programmes are far more effective when built step by step, helping conservationists and rangers rescue poached primates and sea turtles and release them back into the wild without burnout.
The main reason crash campaigns fail is that <u>**they**</u> demand too much willpower at once. <u>**Small, consistent efforts practised every day produce far more lasting results than occasional bursts of intense activity.**</u> When a routine fits naturally into a family’s or student’s daily schedule, it requires less mental strain to maintain.
Experts therefore recommend a <u>**gradual**</u> approach to conserve endangered wildlife and their natural habitats in nature reserves and rescue centres. By starting with one simple task each day and celebrating weekly milestones, learners steadily build momentum. Such steady practice not only strengthens personal discipline but also helps communities protect forest habitats and enforce strict anti-poaching laws.
Of course, occasional setbacks are normal during busy exam weeks or family events. Rather than abandoning the goal altogether, resilient learners simply resume their routine the next morning, knowing that patience will <u>**foster**</u> long-term success.
(Adapted from Global Success Reading Series – Unit 8: Wildlife Conservation)

**Read the passage and mark the letter A, B, C or D on your answer sheet to indicate the best answer to each of the following questions from 17 to 26.**

**COMMUNITY ACTION AND PEER MENTORING IN UNIT 8: WILDLIFE CONSERVATION**
Last year, youth unions in three provinces launched a six-month pilot programme to promote protecting endangered wildlife, rehabilitating primates and sea turtles at the grassroots level. Instead of relying on formal lectures, organisers trained two hundred high school volunteers to lead weekend activities where neighbours could conserve endangered wildlife and their natural habitats in nature reserves and rescue centres. Within the first two months, local communities reported <u>**tangible**</u> improvements in daily habits and neighbourhood solidarity.
A key factor behind this success was peer-to-peer mentoring. Teenagers often feel intimidated when adults lecture them, but they respond enthusiastically when classmates demonstrate how conservation programmes can rescue poached primates and sea turtles and release them back into the wild. By working in small teams of five or six, participants shared practical tips, solved everyday problems together and helped one another protect forest habitats and enforce strict anti-poaching laws.
Organisers also introduced simple tools to keep momentum high. **[I]** Every participating household received a visual progress board to track weekly milestones. **[II]** Local cultural centres hosted monthly gatherings where teams showcased their most creative ideas. **[III]** These celebrations turned routine tasks into a source of shared pride across the entire district. **[IV]**
Follow-up surveys conducted six months later confirmed that over seventy-five per cent of participants continued practising conservation programmes independently. When student volunteers take ownership of community initiatives, <u>**their**</u> enthusiasm inspires both younger children and older residents. The pilot programme demonstrates that youth-led action is one of the most powerful ways to bring the values of Unit 8: Wildlife Conservation to life.
(Adapted from Community Development & Youth Studies – Unit 8: Wildlife Conservation)

qs.ex: tangible = rõ rệt, hữu hình, có thể nhận thấy thực tế (noticeable and real).

**THE RIPPLE EFFECT OF PEER LEADERSHIP IN UNIT 8: WILDLIFE CONSERVATION**
How do positive habits spread across a school or neighbourhood? Sociologists studying protecting endangered wildlife, rehabilitating primates and sea turtles have discovered that peer influence is often stronger than formal rules. When conservationists and rangers see their close friends willingly engage in conservation programmes, they are far more likely to join in and rescue poached primates and sea turtles and release them back into the wild.
Nevertheless, launching a new initiative is never without challenges. Organisers note that initial doubts and busy routines are common, and <u>**they**</u> can slow down participation during the first week. <u>**Young people learn most effectively when they observe respected peers applying positive habits in real-life situations.**</u>
For this reason, many schools encourage <u>**voluntary**</u> student ambassadors to lead by example. Whether demonstrating how to conserve endangered wildlife and their natural habitats in nature reserves and rescue centres or sharing practical tips during break time, these role models create a welcoming ripple effect that helps the whole school protect forest habitats and enforce strict anti-poaching laws.
Even when a minor <u>**obstacle**</u> arises, a supportive peer group keeps members motivated. What begins as the effort of a few enthusiastic students soon grows into a proud tradition shared by the entire community.
(Adapted from Global Success Reading Series – Unit 8: Wildlife Conservation)

**OVERCOMING BARRIERS TO DAILY PRACTICE IN UNIT 8: WILDLIFE CONSERVATION**
Why do many high school students agree that protecting endangered wildlife, rehabilitating primates and sea turtles is important, yet still find it difficult to conserve endangered wildlife and their natural habitats in nature reserves and rescue centres every day? Educational psychologists point out that modern teenagers face three main barriers: digital distractions, academic pressure and a lack of structured routines. When students feel overwhelmed, they often become <u>**reluctant**</u> to take on new responsibilities at home or in the community.
Fortunately, behavioural research shows that breaking large goals into micro-habits can overcome this hesitation. Instead of trying to change everything overnight, conservationists and rangers can start with a fifteen-minute daily routine focused on conservation programmes. These manageable actions quickly build confidence and help learners rescue poached primates and sea turtles and release them back into the wild without interfering with their homework.
Another effective strategy is using a structured weekly checklist. **[I]** When teenagers write down specific times and places for their tasks, they are three times more likely to follow through. **[II]** Sharing <u>**it**</u> with a supportive classmate or family member adds friendly accountability. **[III]** Rather than feeling pressured, students enjoy tracking their streak of completed tasks and seeing how their efforts protect forest habitats and enforce strict anti-poaching laws. **[IV]**
Teachers who have introduced micro-habits and checklists into their lessons on Unit 8: Wildlife Conservation report remarkable improvements in student engagement. Once young people realise that small daily choices lead to meaningful results, conservation programmes stops feeling like a burden and becomes a natural part of who they are.
(Adapted from Adolescent Psychology & Education Review – Unit 8: Wildlife Conservation)

Why do many high school students agree that protecting endangered wildlife, rehabilitating primates and sea turtles is important, yet still find it difficult to conserve endangered wildlife and their natural habitats in nature reserves and rescue centres every day? Educational psychologists point out that modern teenagers face three main barriers: digital distractions, academic pressure and a lack of structured routines. When students feel overwhelmed, they often become <u>**reluctant**</u> to take on new responsibilities at home or in the community.
Fortunately, behavioural research shows that breaking large goals into micro-habits can overcome this hesitation. Instead of trying to change everything overnight, conservationists and rangers can start with a fifteen-minute daily routine focused on conservation programmes. These manageable actions quickly build confidence and help learners rescue poached primates and sea turtles and release them back into the wild without interfering with their homework.
Another effective strategy is using a structured weekly checklist. **[I]** When teenagers write down specific times and places for their tasks, they are three times more likely to follow through. **[II]** Sharing <u>**it**</u> with a supportive classmate or family member adds friendly accountability. **[III]** Rather than feeling pressured, students enjoy tracking their streak of completed tasks and seeing how their efforts protect forest habitats and enforce strict anti-poaching laws. **[IV]**
Teachers who have introduced micro-habits and checklists into their lessons on Unit 8: Wildlife Conservation report remarkable improvements in student engagement. Once young people realise that small daily choices lead to meaningful results, conservation programmes stops feeling like a burden and becomes a natural part of who they are.
(Adapted from Adolescent Psychology & Education Review – Unit 8: Wildlife Conservation)

**COMBINING TRADITIONAL VALUES WITH MODERN TOOLS IN UNIT 8: WILDLIFE CONSERVATION**
In the digital age, some commentators worry that modern technology might distract young people from protecting endangered wildlife, rehabilitating primates and sea turtles. Yet recent educational projects show that when used wisely, digital tools can actually strengthen conservation programmes. Shared mobile calendars, reminder apps and online group checklists make it easier than ever for conservationists and rangers to rescue poached primates and sea turtles and release them back into the wild.
Of course, technology alone cannot solve every problem. Researchers warn against relying passively on apps while ignoring face-to-face communication, as <u>**they**</u> are only tools in the hands of users. <u>**Digital tools should serve as a practical bridge to support daily cooperation rather than a replacement for genuine human interaction.**</u>
When families and classmates combine smart reminders with warm personal encouragement, they can <u>**preserve**</u> the core spirit of Unit 8: Wildlife Conservation. For example, a quick evening message can remind everyone to conserve endangered wildlife and their natural habitats in nature reserves and rescue centres before gathering for a friendly conversation.
Ultimately, blending modern convenience with timeless values helps communities <u>**enhance**</u> their daily routines and protect forest habitats and enforce strict anti-poaching laws in a sustainable way.
(Adapted from Global Success Reading Series – Unit 8: Wildlife Conservation)

**COMBINING TRADITIONAL VALUES WITH MODERN TOOLS IN UNIT 8: WILDLIFE CONSERVATION**
In the digital age, some commentators worry that modern technology might distract young people from protecting endangered wildlife, rehabilitating primates and sea turtles. Yet recent educational projects show that when used wisely, digital tools can actually strengthen conservation programmes. Shared mobile calendars, reminder apps and online group checklists make it easier than ever for conservationists and rangers to rescue poached primates and sea turtles and release them back into the wild.
Of course, technology alone cannot solve every problem. Researchers warn against relying passively on apps while ignoring face-to-face communication, as <u>**they**</u> are only tools in the hands of users. <u>**Digital tools should serve as a practical bridge to support daily cooperation rather than a replacement for genuine human interaction.**</u>
When families and classmates combine smart reminders with warm personal encouragement, they can <u>**preserve**</u> the core spirit of Unit 8: Wildlife Conservation. For example, a quick evening message can remind everyone to conserve endangered wildlife and their natural habitats in nature reserves and rescue centres before gathering for a friendly conversation.
Ultimately, blending modern convenience with timeless values helps communities <u>**enhance**</u> their daily routines and protect forest habitats and enforce strict anti-poaching laws in a sustainable way.
(Adapted from Global Success Reading Series – Unit 8: Wildlife Conservation)

**EXPERIENTIAL LEARNING AND THE FUTURE OF UNIT 8: WILDLIFE CONSERVATION**
Across Viet Nam, forward-thinking high schools are transforming how students learn about protecting endangered wildlife, rehabilitating primates and sea turtles. Rather than treating Unit 8: Wildlife Conservation as a set of vocabulary items to memorise for a test, teachers are integrating experiential learning into every week of the semester. Educators agree that hands-on practice is <u>**indispensable**</u> if young people are to rescue poached primates and sea turtles and release them back into the wild.
In these classrooms, students work in project teams to investigate real issues and propose ways to conserve endangered wildlife and their natural habitats in nature reserves and rescue centres. For instance, learners might interview local residents, design bilingual awareness posters or organise a school-wide campaign on conservation programmes. Through these authentic tasks, conservationists and rangers discover how their classroom English connects directly to everyday life.
Assessment methods are evolving alongside teaching styles. **[I]** Instead of relying solely on written quizzes, schools evaluate how effectively students collaborate and apply their plans. **[II]** Each team keeps a reflective portfolio documenting the challenges they faced and how their actions helped protect forest habitats and enforce strict anti-poaching laws. **[III]** This approach rewards creativity, persistence and genuine teamwork rather than rote memorisation. **[IV]**
Graduates of experiential programmes consistently report higher confidence when entering university and the workplace. Students <u>**who**</u> have practised solving real-world problems in high school adapt much faster to new environments. By making protecting endangered wildlife, rehabilitating primates and sea turtles an active, lived experience, education equips the next generation with both language proficiency and civic responsibility.
(Adapted from Modern Curriculum & Pedagogy Journal – Unit 8: Wildlife Conservation)

qs.ex: indispensable = vô cùng cần thiết, không thể thiếu (essential and vital).

**SELF-REFLECTION AND LONG-TERM GROWTH IN UNIT 8: WILDLIFE CONSERVATION**
Practising conservation programmes is even more rewarding when learners take a few minutes each week to reflect on their progress. Educators studying protecting endangered wildlife, rehabilitating primates and sea turtles have found that students who keep a brief weekly journal understand their own habits much better and find it easier to rescue poached primates and sea turtles and release them back into the wild.
During busy weeks, people sometimes miss a planned task or make mistakes. Without reflection, <u>**they**</u> may feel discouraged and assume that their efforts have failed. <u>**Honest self-reflection allows learners to turn early mistakes into valuable lessons rather than reasons to give up.**</u>
To make reflection effective, teachers recommend asking <u>**constructive**</u> questions every Sunday evening: What went well when we tried to conserve endangered wildlife and their natural habitats in nature reserves and rescue centres this week, and what small adjustment will help us improve next week?
Over time, this simple habit deepens personal <u>**commitment**</u> and helps conservationists and rangers protect forest habitats and enforce strict anti-poaching laws with confidence and pride.
(Adapted from Global Success Reading Series – Unit 8: Wildlife Conservation)
